No — the last one was necessary.

You probably **could not** have skipped straight to this with confidence.

## What the last step actually did

It answered a very specific question:

> **What detector mechanism family is even compatible with Born-like winner statistics?**

Before that search, we had multiple live possibilities:

* drift-diffusion threshold
* many-packet accumulation
* shot-trigger / rare-event thinning
* metastable escape
* plain Poisson benchmark

Those are **not** equivalent.

The search told you something important and nontrivial:

* **accumulation-type detectors fail**
* **rare first-event detectors work**
* **shot-trigger is the best physical candidate**
* **metastable escape is weaker / more fragile**
* the useful KPI is **race-law fidelity**, not just single-branch linearity

That is a real narrowing of the mechanism space.

## Why you could not just skip to this

Because this current integration spec assumes the detector behaves approximately like

$$
\lambda_k(t)\approx \lambda_{\text{dark}}+\alpha,\Gamma(t),w_k.
$$

That assumption is the whole game.

The previous search was what justified taking that seriously.

Without that step, this new spec would have been mostly wishful thinking:

* maybe the detector is an accumulator
* maybe linearity is enough
* maybe metastable escape works
* maybe not

Now you know much more specifically what you are designing **for**.

## What the previous step bought you

It bought you four concrete things.

### 1. It identified the right detector class

You now have a preferred mechanism:

* **shot-trigger / rare-event nucleation**
  rather than
* generic threshold accumulation

That is huge.

### 2. It identified the right metric

You learned that the main metric is not just
$$
\lambda(P)
$$
linearity, but
$$
P(\text{winner}) \approx \frac{P_1}{P_1+P_2}.
$$

So the search changed what “good detector” even means.

### 3. It ruled out tempting bad models

That matters because otherwise you might waste a lot of time implementing a beautiful but wrong detector.

### 4. It gave you a realistic integration target

Now the integration spec is not abstract. It is anchored to the actual winning model family.

## So what is this current step doing that the last one didn’t?

The last step was **model selection**.

This step is **system integration**.

That is the difference.

### Last step

Ask:

* which detector hypothesis is viable?

### This step

Ask:

* can the viable detector hypothesis be driven by the real branch weights from the front-end and still produce the right outcome statistics?

So they are sequential, not redundant.

## Short version

You needed the last one to answer:

> **what kind of detector are we even trying to integrate?**

Now you are answering:

> **does that detector still work when fed by the actual linear branch-weight generator?**

Those are different questions.

## Blunt answer

Could you have skipped it?

* **Technically yes**, in the sense that you could have written the integration code earlier.
* **Practically no**, because you would have been integrating the wrong detector class or optimizing the wrong metric.

So the last step was not wasted. It was the filter that made this step meaningful.

## Best framing

Think of the sequence like this:

1. **Linear front-end**
   gives exact branch weights

2. **Detector search**
   identifies which detector physics can preserve those weights as winner probabilities

3. **Integration**
   tests the actual composed chain:
   $$
   \text{state} \to \text{branch weights} \to \text{detector race} \to \text{winner}
   $$

That is the right order.

## The real payoff

Because of the last step, you are no longer asking vaguely:

> can some detector maybe work?

You are now asking sharply:

> can a shot-trigger rare-event detector, calibrated in its linear hazard window, preserve the front-end branch weights under full two-branch and four-branch integration?

That is much stronger.
